claim: Simple one-reason or unit-weight rules (take-the-best, tallying) match or beat multiple regression out of sample on small real data sets, while looking up far fewer cues (2.4 vs 7.7 on average over 20 data sets).
agent_test: On a fixed benchmark, compare a 2-3 cue checklist decision against a full-rubric weighted decision at equal tokens, scored on held-out items.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The accuracy edge of simple rules comes from variance reduction (bias-variance trade-off) and is largest with small training samples; with enough data, flexible models catch up. Fast-and-frugal trees are competitive with ML (balanced accuracy .83 vs SVM .86, RLR .83, RF .83), not better.
agent_test: Vary the number of worked examples or retrieved cases given to the agent (few vs many) and check where a simple-rule mode stops winning.
audit_note: Balanced accuracies .86/.83/.83/.83 verified (SVM crashed on two sets); note Gigerenzer & Brighton's cross-validated city task shows take-the-best ahead across all sizes, so 'flexible models catch up' is the general bias-variance argument, not that figure.

claim: Which strategy wins depends on environment structure (ecological rationality): take-the-best at noncompensatory or highly variable cue validities and low sample size; tallying at low predictability, few objects per cue and correlated cues.
agent_test: Tag benchmark items by structure (dominant cue vs many weak cues) and check that routing to simple vs deliberate mode by that tag beats a fixed mode.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The less-is-more effect for recognition (knowing less beats knowing more) is a real analytic and simulation result (peak about 77% at partial knowledge in the 1996 cities simulation) but empirical support in human data is mixed; it needs recognition validity above knowledge validity and is often absent.
agent_test: Not directly testable on an LLM; skip. Use only as a warning against assuming less information is always better.

claim: People use the recognition heuristic selectively: adherence drops when recognition is not tied to the criterion (54% for distance vs 89% for population in Pohl 2006; about 30% choosing the recognized object for Chernobyl vs a fictitious city) and when a contradicting cue exists (Richter & Spaeth: mean adherence 95% to 82%, median unchanged at 97%; Newell & Fernandez: 98% to 64%).
schema_part: G (do not trust a familiarity signal blindly)
agent_test: Check whether the agent's reliance on a retrieved or familiar answer changes with a stated or measured validity of that signal.
audit_note: 54% vs 89% (Pohl 2006) and about 30% (Oppenheimer) check out, but the contradicting-cue figure is 95% to 82% mean (Richter & Spaeth; median stayed 97%); 98% belongs to Newell & Fernandez, where it fell to 64%.
claim_before_audit: People use the recognition heuristic selectively: adherence drops when recognition is not tied to the criterion (54% distance vs 89% population; about 30% for Chernobyl vs fictitious city) and when contradicting cues exist (98% to 82%).

claim: Group-level adherence to the recognition heuristic (about 91 percent, unverified on re-check) overstates pure rule use: a multinomial model gives true use r about .80, and about 71 percent of individuals (20 of 28) differ reliably from pure use. Defenders reply that group means hide a minority of strict users (17 of 28 followed it at most once wrongly in 32 trials in one study).
agent_test: When measuring a mode on an agent, report per-item usage, not only averages.

claim: Frugal does not mean fast for humans: under a 2000 ms deadline take-the-best was slower and less compliant than tallying in one experiment, reversed with reformatted stimuli. Cue count is not a proxy for time cost. In LLM agents the token cost is large and measurable: o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional ones on 2+3 (Chen 2025); latency was not measured.
agent_test: Measure real tokens and latency of a few-cue mode vs a many-cue mode rather than assuming savings from fewer cues.

claim: Strategy use is learned from feedback and adapts to environment: take-the-best-consistent choices rose from 28 to 71 percent in a high-variability environment and fell to 12 percent in a low-variability one; 87 of 99 people changed recognition reliance between domains. But individual-level compliance in early tests was low (3 of 16 searched in validity order).
agent_test: Let the agent update which mode it picks from outcome feedback over a run and compare with a fixed mode at equal tokens.

claim: Fast-and-frugal trees give transparent decision rules of about 2 cues that do about as well as logistic regression or ML in medicine, bail, software defects, but regression slightly beat them in at least one expert-judgment dataset and many comparisons were fits rather than predictions.
agent_test: Build a 3-question yes/no tree that decides which mode to run; compare to an LLM-chosen mode at equal tokens.

claim: Longer chain of thought hurts accuracy on items where the right answer is that the question cannot be determined (17.3 point median drop, 95 percent CrI 7.7 to 25.5; strong in mid-size Qwen models, directional in GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5, reversed in Phi-3.5). Author ties this to take-the-best by theory only. Independent support in direction: reasoning models over-think and abstain less on missing-premise or unanswerable items (Fan 2025; AbstentionBench, 20 models, -24% abstention recall). Not an exact replication of Bogdan's items.
agent_test: Replicate with our own indeterminate-answer items, direct vs stepwise at equal tokens, on our model.

claim: CoT helps mainly on math and symbolic tasks (average gains 12.3 points for math and 14.2 for symbolic); elsewhere direct answering is near equal, and as much as 95 percent of the MMLU gain is on questions containing an equals sign. This supports a gate that skips deliberation on non-symbolic items.
agent_test: Run direct vs stepwise by task class on our benchmark and fit the S0 gate on class, at equal tokens.
audit_note: Sprague et al. give average CoT gains of 14.2 for symbolic, 12.3 for math, 6.9 for logical; the claim swaps the labels. The 95% MMLU equals-sign figure is confirmed.
claim_before_audit: CoT helps mainly on math and symbolic tasks (average gains 14.2 and 12.3 points); elsewhere direct answering is near equal, and as much as 95 percent of the MMLU gain is on questions containing an equals sign. This supports a gate that skips deliberation on non-symbolic items.

claim: Deliberation can reduce accuracy in specific LLM tasks that mirror human verbal-overshadowing: GPT-4o on implicit pattern learning fell from 87.5 to 64.4 percent with CoT (-23.1); face recognition fell for all 6 models; inverse scaling in test-time compute appears on distractor and spurious-feature tasks.
agent_test: Include perception-like and spurious-feature items in the test set and check that the gate routes them to direct mode.

claim: Cheap-first cascades and routers keep most quality at much lower cost (FrugalGPT up to 98 percent cost cut at GPT-4 accuracy; RouteLLM 95 percent of GPT-4 quality at reduced strong-model calls; AdaptThink length -53 percent, accuracy +2.4 percent): the machine analogue of stop-at-first-discriminating-cue.
agent_test: Cascade: answer direct, escalate to full schema only when a cheap confidence check fails; compare to always-full at equal total tokens.
audit_note: RouteLLM's 95% of GPT-4 is the MT Bench figure (8.8 vs 9.3); GSM8K at the same point is 87%, so the evidence note saying GSM8K 95% is wrong, but the claim does not rely on it.

claim: LLM-written simple rules or greedy no-backtrack trees do not automatically replicate the FFT advantage: LLM IF-THEN rules reached 80.3 (Claude Sonnet 4.6) and 70.5 percent (GPT-4o) on UCI heart disease vs 90.2 for random forest; walking an LLM-built tree with a VLM lost to zero-shot in 12 of 12 pairs.
agent_test: If a tree gate is used, derive cue order from data (validities) not from the LLM's own guess.
audit_note: Numbers verified (RF 90.2, Sonnet 4.6 rules 80.3, GPT-4o rules 70.5; 12 of 12 pairs below zero-shot); the studies test LLM rules and trees generally, not fast-and-frugal trees as such.

claim: Tuning-installed heuristics in LLMs are measurable: instruction-tuned or RLHF models show higher certainty-effect and belief-bias scores than their pretrained counterparts (decoy-effect results are mixed, and RLHF cannot be isolated from instruction tuning), and across 15 base/tuned pairs instruction tuning made number choice less uniform in all 15, with tuned models almost never returning the endpoints (median ratio to interior rate near 0 vs 0.30-0.60 for base). Scale changes human-like heuristic errors non-monotonically (CRT: davinci-003 5 percent, ChatGPT-3.5 59, ChatGPT-4 96).
agent_test: Model-specific: probe our model with a few classic items before relying on any heuristic-based design.
audit_note: Itzhak et al. find decoy effects mixed (and the T5 to Flan-T5 certainty rise not significant) and cannot separate RLHF from instruction tuning; Ansari's 15 of 15 is for distributions becoming less uniform, while endpoint avoidance is reported as medians (base already avoids endpoints at 0.30-0.60 of interior rate, tuned near 0).
claim_before_audit: Tuning-installed heuristics in LLMs are measurable: instruction tuning and RLHF raise decoy, certainty and belief bias, and tuned models avoid endpoints in number choice in 15 of 15 base/tuned pairs. Scale changes human-like heuristic errors non-monotonically (CRT: davinci-003 5 percent, ChatGPT-3.5 59, ChatGPT-4 96).

claim: No published study found runs the founding paradigms (city-size paired comparison, cue-ordered take-the-best, FFT construction from cue validities) on LLMs; the only LLM paper tied to take-the-best is a single-author preprint. Re-checked by the gap search: about 28 more arXiv queries found none. Peer-reviewed venues were not searched (quota).
agent_test: We could run this ourselves: cue-ordered paired comparisons with the LLM seeing only k cues.

claim: Learned take-the-best variants recover cue order from data: ABC-TTB (Schulz et al. 2016) outperforms classic TTB and CART on the 81-city data set (read from a figure) and recovers simulated TTB structure, and probabilistic TTB (Peltola et al. 2019) performs comparably or better than classic TTB and ABC-TTB and better than logistic regression on three of four small benchmarks (homeless, profsalary, city; logistic regression wins on mileage, the largest). These are model papers on few benchmark data sets, with Peltola's reusing Schulz's data.
agent_test: Learn cue validities for gate features from a calibration set, then use them to order checks.
audit_note: Schulz et al. (2016) test only the 81-city data (plus simulated data) and compare TTB, ABC-TTB and CART, not logistic regression; the four datasets (homeless, profsalary, city, mileage) and the logistic-regression comparison are Peltola et al. (2019), where regression wins on mileage.
claim_before_audit: Learned take-the-best variants (ABC-TTB, probabilistic TTB) recover cue order and direction from data and match or beat classic TTB and often logistic regression on small benchmarks, but they are model papers on the same four to five benchmark data sets.

claim: More reasoning is not safe on unanswerable or ill-posed items: reasoning models write much longer answers on missing-premise questions (Fan et al.), reasoning fine-tuning lowers abstention by 24% on average across 20 LLMs (Kirichenko et al.), and bigger reasoning budgets in a sweep on two models did not improve abstention (no gain on GSM8k-Abstain, a decline on UMWP) while accuracy rose. Two independent groups, same direction, different designs.
schema_part: S0 gate / G (route indeterminate items to a short check)
agent_test: Run the same 'cannot be determined' items with direct, short CoT and long CoT on our model and count abstentions.
audit_note: AbstentionBench's budget sweep (s1.1 32B, R1 Distill 'same trend') shows abstention not improving on GSM8k-Abstain and worsening on UMWP while accuracy rises, and o1 reasoning effort was mixed, so 'generally worsen' is too strong.
claim_before_audit: More reasoning is not safe on unanswerable or ill-posed items: reasoning-tuned models write much longer answers and abstain less, and bigger reasoning budgets generally worsen abstention. Two independent groups, same direction, different designs.

claim: LLMs carry usable familiarity signals: an internal known/unknown entity direction (causal for refusal), semantic entropy from sample disagreement (probe AUROC 0.7 to 0.95) and trained P(IK). But confidence informativeness is domain-specific and not tied to accuracy (factor 1.98 across models; rank correlation with accuracy -0.80 on TriviaQA vs +0.00 on Natural Questions), mirroring the human 54% vs 89% recognition split. None of these was tested as a take-the-best cue.
schema_part: G (do not trust one cue without domain validity)
agent_test: Measure, per task class, the AUROC of self-consistency agreement as a predictor of correctness. Use it as a gate only where AUROC is high.
audit_note: Numbers verified in v3 of the metacognition paper (rho -0.80 TriviaQA, +0.00 NQ over four models, 1.98-fold); the 'mirrors human 54% vs 89%' link is the researcher's analogy, not a source finding.

claim: The value of a correct skip is large and measurable: o1-like models spend 1,953% more tokens on 2+3, the first round is right in over 92% of correct cases, and a trained gate cuts long thinking by 50 to 90% with accuracy near flat. The false-skip cost is not reported in a comparable form, so it still has to be measured.
agent_test: Log tokens and correctness for direct vs full schema per item, then compute the break-even false-skip rate.
audit_note: Per-benchmark Thinkless accuracy checked only on GSM8K (0.8418 vs 0.8347 for the R1-1.5B baseline); 1,953% and over-92% figures verified in Chen et al.

claim: Giving the model less can help: irrelevant context sharply cuts accuracy (no more than 18% of baseline-solved problems stay solved under all distractor types). This is indirect support for a cue-limited prompt. No study tests top-k validity-ordered cues at equal tokens.
agent_test: Run top-k cue prompts vs all-cue prompts on the city-size paired comparison and one new task.

claim: LLMs can learn numeric cue weights in context from about 50 examples and rival Random Forest or gradient boosting, so learning cue validities in context is plausible. Whether they learn a noncompensatory cue order (take-the-best) or default to compensatory weighting on binary cues is untested; no LLM run of the Rieskamp-Otto paradigm was found.
agent_test: Give 8, 16 and 32 labelled pairs with binary cues. Check whether choices follow the first discriminating cue or a weighted sum.

claim: On the founding city example, out-of-sample margins between take-the-best, regression and unit-weight are under one point (72.2 / 71.9 / 71.4 per a secondary source). Exact 20-data-set Czerlinski percentages were not found in any open text. The claim stays: parity at far lower cost, not a large win.
agent_test: Do not quote percentages from the 1999 chapter. Cite the parity result and the cue counts (2.4 vs 7.7).

claim: The LLM work reachable on this topic tests heuristics and biases (anchoring, framing, endowment, with human matches), not the adaptive toolbox. No study in Judgment and Decision Making, Cognition or Psychological Review on LLM ecological rationality was found, but peer-reviewed venues were not searchable (quota).
agent_test: Treat the field as open and plan own experiments.
